title: Weather Card
blurb: Make city cards from JSON weather data
intro: This time you'll make weather cards! The file weather.json has the sky, temperature and chance of rain for each city (made-up practice data). You'll read it with Chapter 14's JSON and show the chosen city as a neat card with Chapter 1's alignment formats.
finale: You did it! Type a city name and pull up its card. If you add cities to weather.json, the list and cards grow all by themselves.

play.prompt: Type the name of a city to see its weather

tool.title: New tool: json.load
tool.body: Chapter 14's json.loads turned JSON text into a dictionary. json.load(f) reads the file f you opened with with and turns it straight into a dictionary. It does json.loads(f.read()) in one go.
tool.code:
import json

with open("menu.json") as f:
    menu = json.load(f)
print(menu["latte"])

steps.solution:
import json

with open("weather.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(f"Cities in the file: {len(data)}")
for city in data:
    print("-", city)
print("Which city?")
city = input()
info = data[city]
print(f"Sky: {info['sky']}")
print(f"Temp: {info['temp']}C")
steps.explain: You took values out twice: once from the outer dictionary by city, then from the inner one by sky and temp. That's how you read nested data.

steps.task: Replace the two prints under info = data[city] with five card lines. The first line centers the city name between = signs with {city:=^14}. The Sky, Temp and Rain lines put the value in 6 right-aligned spaces after the label, like "Sky  " then {info['sky']:>6}. Add "C" after Temp, "%" after Rain (info['rain']), and the last line is "=" * 14.

hints: :=^14 centers in 14 spaces and fills the gaps with =. :>6 right-aligns in 6 spaces (Chapter 1's formats).
Use :>6 for all three values so the numbers line up. Labels are 5 characters wide: "Sky" gets two spaces after it, "Temp" and "Rain" one.
steps.solution:
import json

with open("weather.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(f"Cities in the file: {len(data)}")
for city in data:
    print("-", city)
print("Which city?")
city = input()
info = data[city]
print(f"{city:=^14}")
print(f"Sky  {info['sky']:>6}")
print(f"Temp {info['temp']:>6}C")
print(f"Rain {info['rain']:>6}%")
print("=" * 14)
steps.explain: The :>6 format right-aligns the values, so the numbers stand in a neat column. Long or short, the city's title line is always 14 wide.

hints: city in data tells you True or False: is that key in the dictionary? (Chapter 8)
It's in data, not in data.values(). City names are the keys.
steps.solution:
import json

with open("weather.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)
print(f"Cities in the file: {len(data)}")
for city in data:
    print("-", city)
print("Which city?")
city = input()
if city in data:
    info = data[city]
    print(f"{city:=^14}")
    print(f"Sky  {info['sky']:>6}")
    print(f"Temp {info['temp']:>6}C")
    print(f"Rain {info['rain']:>6}%")
    print("=" * 14)
else:
    print("No weather for that city")
steps.explain: Asking whether the key exists before taking it out prevents the KeyError. Next time you could also try catching it with try and except KeyError (this step practices if). Now no name can stop the program!
